Aims The potential of mechanistic biomarkers to improve prediction of drug‐induced liver injury (DILI) and hepatic regeneration is widely acknowledged. We sought to determine reference intervals for new biomarkers of DILI and regeneration, as well as to characterize their natural variability and impact of diurnal variation. Methods Serum samples from 227 healthy volunteers were recruited as part of a cross‐sectional study; of these, 25 subjects had weekly serial sampling over 3 weeks, while 23 had intensive blood sampling over a 24h period. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), MicroRNA‐122 (miR‐122), High Mobility Group Box‐1 (HMGB1), total Keratin‐18 (K18), caspase‐cleaved Keratin‐18 (ccK18), Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GLDH) and Macrophage Colony‐Stimulating Factor‐1 (CSF‐1) were assayed. Results Reference intervals were established for each biomarker based on the 97.5% quantile (90% CI) following the assessment of fixed effects in univariate and multivariable models. Intra‐individual variability was found to be non‐significant, and there was no significant impact of diurnal variation. Conclusion Reference intervals for novel DILI biomarkers have been described. An upper limit of a reference range might represent the most appropriate mechanism to utilize these data. What is already known about this subject Potential for novel biomarkers to improve prediction of drug‐induced liver injury (DILI) is widely acknowledged. It is necessary that reference intervals for these biomarkers are defined in several healthy human populations. What this study adds Our study reports reference intervals for novel biomarkers of DILI in healthy volunteers. We report a reference interval for biomarker HGMB1 in healthy volunteers. Data will be a useful point of reference when interpreting exploratory clinical DILI studies. Data can also be used when seeking biomarker qualification by regulatory authorities. 1 INTRODUCTION Drug‐induced liver injury (DILI) represents a major cause of patient morbidity and mortality and is a serious concern for patients, clinicians and the pharmaceutical industry. 1 , 2 It accounts for over half of the acute liver failure cases observed in Western countries and is a leading cause of withdrawal postmarketing. 1 , 2 Assessment of liver injury and repair has to date relied on a small number of blood‐based markers. These include serum alanine and aspartate aminotransferase activity (ALT and AST, respectively) as indicators of hepatocellular injury; alkaline phosphatase (ALP), γ‐glutamyl transferase (GGT) and total bilirubin (TBIL) for assessment of cholestatic injury; prothrombin time as a marker of liver synthetic capacity. 3 , 4 However, the lack of sensitivity and specificity of these tests, together with the fact that they provide little information about the mechanistic basis of liver injury, are significant limitations in using them for prediction and understanding DILI. Furthermore, elevation of these markers can be a result of disease/injury in nonhepatic sites, 5 and the markers are of limited prognostic value. A number of new biomarkers have shown promise in exploratory studies and preliminary evaluations, using samples from patients with liver injury during clinical trials and clinical practice. 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 These include biomarkers that provide enhanced hepatic specificity such as microRNA‐122 (miR‐122), 11 biomarkers that can be used to monitor apoptotic‐necrotic dynamics such as keratin‐18 (K18), caspase‐cleaved K18 (ccK18) 9 , 10 and high mobility group box‐1 (HMGB1), mitochondrial dysfunction (glutamate dehydrogenase; GLDH), 8 , 9 and proteins that promote hepatic regeneration such as macrophage colony‐stimulating factor (CSF‐1). Both miR‐122 and GLDH are potential liver‐specific alternatives to ALT, having performed well as biomarkers for hepatocellular injury, particularly in patients with DILI resulting from paracetamol overdose 12 , 13 , 14 . The measurement of apoptotic vs . necrotic cell death using circulating K18 levels has also provided insights into the mechanistic basis of DILI in man. 8 , 15 Recent work has demonstrated the potential utility of these novel biomarkers, with a 3‐biomarker multivariate linear regression model achieving near perfect separation between patients with liver damage following paracetamol overdose and healthy controls (receiver operator characteristic, area under the curve = 0.99). 10 Furthermore, this 3‐biomarker model confirmed strong predictability and specificity when comparing patients with liver damage to patient cohorts with muscle, pancreas, gastrointestinal and kidney damage (receiver operator characteristic, area under the curve = 0.98). 10 Based on these observations, there has been significant interest and investment by biomarker consortia and DILI researcher networks to further develop and qualify novel DILI biomarker candidates that can add value, including mechanistic understanding, to current assessment methods. Importantly, these candidate biomarkers have been underpinned by supportive preclinical science 9 , 16 , 17 and more recently, letters of support from regulatory authorities have backed the continued development and qualification of these candidate biomarkers across the spectrum of DILI observed in man. 13 , 14 Reference intervals in healthy volunteers were first reported by Church et al . as part of a larger investigation into the aforementioned biomarkers as candidate biomarkers for DILI. 9 K18, ccK18 and miR‐122 levels in many healthy volunteers were found to be below the lower limit of quantification. Furthermore, miR‐122 demonstrated high inter‐ and intrasubject variability, which raised questions about its application and interpretation as a candidate biomarker for DILI. Given the potential utility of these biomarkers, it is important that reference intervals are defined in several healthy human populations, to aid further qualification of new biomarkers of liver injury or regeneration, so they can be appropriately interpreted in patients with DILI. As such, the aim of this current investigation was to establish reference intervals for miR122, GLDH, K18, ccK18, HMGB1 and CSF‐1, in a healthy human volunteer cohort and to assess the impact of inter‐ and intraindividual variation, and diurnal variation.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and hepatic regeneration; assessment of intra- and interindividual variation, and diurnal variation, of biomarkers in healthy volunteers.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: MicroRNA-122 (miR-122) provides enhanced hepatic specificity, and its expression, along with GLDH, is enriched in the liver, with their serum levels potentially influenced by factors like visceral fat and sex. Keratin-18 (K18) and caspase-cleaved K18 (ccK18) monitor apoptotic-necrotic dynamics and reflect the degree of hepatocellular necrotic and/or apoptotic injury. High Mobility Group Box-1 (HMGB1) is also involved in apoptotic-necrotic dynamics. Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GLDH) reflects mitochondrial dysfunction. Macrophage Colony-Stimulating Factor-1 (CSF-1) promotes hepatic regeneration, although its levels may be affected by serum collection methods, suggesting potential loss during the clotting process when collecting serum from whole blood.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study focused on establishing reference ranges for DILI biomarkers in healthy human volunteers under standardized conditions, rather than investigating dose-response effects or comparisons of treatment intensities. Therefore, specific dose-response information related to DILI biomarkers is not applicable within this context.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) lacks liver specificity, as it can be elevated in nonliver diseases such as cardiac injury and skeletal muscle damage. In contrast, MicroRNA-122 (miR-122) and Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GLDH) are advocated as potential liver-specific alternatives. A 3-biomarker model demonstrated strong predictability and specificity, achieving near-perfect separation between patients with liver damage (e.g., from paracetamol overdose) and healthy controls, and distinguishing liver damage from muscle, pancreas, gastrointestinal, and kidney damage. Macrophage Colony-Stimulating Factor-1 (CSF-1) has shown sensitive diagnostic capabilities and increased specificity compared to GM-CSF and IL-3 for patients with pancreatic and ampullary cancer in previous studies.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Healthy human volunteers (aged >=18 years, free from HIV, hepatitis B or C, recent medical intervention, pregnancy, or use of illicit drugs/alcohol/tobacco/paracetamol/strenuous exercise) for establishing biomarker reference intervals. The ultimate clinical application targets patients with drug-induced liver injury (DILI), with an acknowledgment of limited representation of older individuals over 50 years in the healthy volunteer cohort. In a broader context, CSF-1 has relevance for patients with pancreatic and ampullary cancer.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is a major cause of patient morbidity and mortality. Novel mechanism-based biomarkers of liver injury and regeneration possess significant potential and clinical validity to complement current liver function tests. They can offer an early indication of hepatocyte damage in acute settings and provide enhanced liver specificity, addressing an unmet need for improved DILI biomarker specificity and sensitivity to predict onset, progression, and treatment response. Establishing reliable reference intervals in healthy individuals is foundational for their future clinical application and interpretation in DILI patients.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: The establishment of reference intervals is crucial for the diagnostic utility of novel DILI biomarkers and in identifying adverse risks associated with DILI. CSF-1 also demonstrates diagnostic utility in the context of pancreatic and ampullary cancer.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The study demonstrated robust reliability for the novel DILI biomarkers (miR-122, K18, ccK18, HMGB1, GLDH, CSF-1) in healthy human volunteers, finding no significant intra-individual variability across all assayed biomarkers in a subset of 25 individuals. No significant diurnal variation was identified over intensive 24-hour sampling. This contradicts previous reports of high miR-122 variability, with this study assessing its intraindividual variability at 41%, significantly lower than a previously reported 94%. Interindividual variability was explored in 227 healthy volunteers, identifying significant fixed effects of sex, BMI, and age on specific biomarkers, necessitating stratified reference ranges. All assays were technically validated, sample processing was standardized, and investigators were blinded. However, variability in mean K18 levels across studies was noted as high due to its ubiquitous expression, and K18/ccK18 levels exhibit relatively high variability in disease states. CSF-1 levels may vary depending on the presence of anticoagulants in blood tubes, suggesting potential loss during clotting. Study limitations include underrepresentation of older individuals, absence of an external validation cohort, and a predominantly Caucasian study population.
recommended_alternatives: Liver-enriched biomarkers (as alternatives to non-specific markers like ALT for enhanced liver specificity)
